title: Shortest Distance After Road Addition Queries I
statement:
Picture `n` cities labelled `0` through `n - 1`. At first the only roads are one-way links from each city `i` to city `i + 1` (for every `i < n - 1`). The pair `queries[i] = [u_i, v_i]` builds one more one-way road, leading from city `u_i` to city `v_i`; roads are built in the order listed and are never taken away.

Each time a road is built, compute the minimum number of roads that a trip from city `0` to city `n - 1` must use. Return these values as the array `answer`, where `answer[i]` is that minimum once the first `i + 1` roads of `queries` exist.

Every query has `v_i - u_i >= 2` (so `u_i < v_i`), and no road is built twice.
constraints: No road appears twice in queries
notes:
## Intuition

Cities and roads form a directed graph in which every road counts as one step, so the fewest roads from city 0 to city `n - 1` is exactly what breadth-first search computes: it reaches cities in order of distance. With at most 500 cities and 500 queries, it is fast enough to add each new road and rerun a full BFS, since one run touches at most `n - 1 + q` roads. (Because every road leads to a larger city, a left-to-right dynamic program over the cities, which is the brute force, gives the same distances.)

## Approach

1. Build the adjacency list `roads` with the starting roads `city → city + 1`.
2. For each query `[u, v]`, append `v` to `roads[u]`.
3. Run BFS from city 0: `dist` is -1 (not reached) everywhere except `dist[0] = 0`. Read cities from `queue` with the index `head`, and give every unreached `neighbor` the distance `dist[city] + 1` before queueing it.
4. Push `dist[n - 1]` onto `answer`.

## Example 1, step by step

`n = 5`. After `[2, 4]`, BFS reaches cities 1, 2, 3 at distances 1, 2, 3 and city 4 at distance 3 through the road `2 → 4`, so the first answer is 3. After `[0, 2]`, city 2 is one road from city 0, so `dist[4] = 2`. After `[0, 4]`, `dist[4] = 1`. The answer is `[3, 2, 1]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(q · (n + q)): one BFS per query over at most `n - 1 + q` roads.
- Space: O(n + q): the adjacency list, `dist` and `queue`.

## Pitfalls

- Roads are one-way: never add the reverse edge `v → u`.
- Earlier roads stay; keep adding to the same graph instead of rebuilding it per query.
- Roads may cross here, so the shortcut from version II of this problem (skipping cities that left the current best route) can be wrong: with `n = 6` and queries `[[1, 4], [0, 2]]` the answers are `[3, 3]`.
- `queue.shift()` costs O(n) in JavaScript; a moving `head` index keeps each BFS linear.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `roads` | `roads[city]` lists the cities one road away from `city` |
| `answer` | the shortest trip length after each query |
| `u`, `v` | start and end of the road built by the current query |
| `dist` | BFS distance from city 0, or -1 when not reached yet |
| `queue`, `head` | the BFS queue and the index of the next city to expand |
| `city`, `neighbor` | the city being expanded and a city one road away from it |

narration.2: Start with the original roads: each city leads to the next one, and the last city leads nowhere.
narration.4: Build the roads in order; earlier roads stay in the graph.
narration.5: Add the new one-way road from u to v.
narration.6: -1 marks cities this BFS has not reached yet.
narration.7: City 0 is the start, at distance 0.
narration.8: The queue starts with city 0 alone.
narration.9: Expand cities in the order they were discovered, which is the order of their distance.
narration.12: The first time BFS reaches a city...
narration.13: ...it got there along a shortest route, one road farther than city.
narration.14: Queue it so the roads leaving it are explored later.
narration.18: Record how many roads the trip to the last city now needs.
narration.20: Return the distance after every query.
